passage: Kalyani, sit. You are upset about your supervisor's shortcuts, and I understand. At twenty-three I found out that my own mentor's site reports had been signed off without visits. I had worshipped that man, and it felt as if the floor had gone. For months I was cold to him and I even threw away my notes from his classes. Then a senior asked me, "Which of the lessons were false?" Honestly, almost none. His way of reading a drawing, of talking with workers, that was real. What was not real was the signing. So I kept the lessons, refused to sign anything I had not checked, and told him quietly that I would not work that way. We were never as close again, and that was all right. Take what is true, Kalyani. Arnab

qa.q: What had the mentor done that let Arnab down at twenty-three?
qa.a: The mentor's site reports had been signed off without visits.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel on discovering it?
qa.a: Arnab felt shocked and betrayed, as if the floor had gone, and turned cold toward the mentor.

qa.q: What did Arnab decide to keep and what to refuse?
qa.a: Arnab kept the true lessons and refused to sign anything that had not been checked.

qa.q: Why might the senior have asked which of the lessons were false?
qa.a: To help Arnab separate the mentor's real teaching from the wrong conduct, instead of rejecting everything.

grounding: An elder recalls learning that a mentor cut corners, keeping the true lessons, holding the mentor as human and refusing the harmful practice.

passage:
At the research institute, Irfan had admired Dr. Charu Mehta since his first year. She had taught him how to design an experiment, how to write, how to stand his ground at conferences.

Then, on a Thursday, he saw her change three numbers in the shared data sheet so the results looked stronger before the grant deadline. The next week, in the corridor, he heard her mock a junior scientist's accent behind his back.

Irfan felt sick. Was everything she taught him a lie?

He sat in the lab after hours, thinking. No. The method she taught him was real. The writing was real. She was also a person who had just done something wrong.

On Monday he went to her office. "Ma'am, I saw the changes in the data sheet. I can't have my name on the grant report with those numbers." She stiffened. "Fine." He also emailed the lab's research integrity officer, briefly and factually.

He kept her notes on experimental design. They were still the best he had.

qa.q: How many numbers did Dr. Mehta change in the data sheet?
What was Irfan feeling after seeing the changes and hearing the mockery?
qa.a: Irfan felt sick and let down, wondering if everything she had taught him was a lie.

qa.q: How did Irfan handle his disillusionment wisely?
qa.a: He kept the lessons that were true, refused to put his name on the altered report, and reported it factually to the integrity officer.

qa.q: How did Dr. Mehta react when Irfan spoke to her?
qa.a: She stiffened and said only "Fine", which suggests she felt caught and defensive.

grounding: The passage shows a young researcher let down when his mentor cuts corners and is petty, who keeps her true lessons and sets a firm boundary on harmful conduct.

passage:
Dear Eshaan sir,

Thank you for the two years of guidance. I mean that before anything else. You taught me how to structure a case, how to read a judge, and how to breathe before standing up.

But I have to tell you something honestly. Last Friday, I heard you tell Mr. Rao that Advocate Sheikh was "a nobody who got lucky", and ask him to delay her client's file out of spite. It was small, and it was unfair to her client, who has done nothing wrong.

I was let down. I've looked up to you more than anyone in this profession.

I've thought about it all weekend. I'm not going to pretend it didn't happen, and I'm not going to throw away everything you taught me either. But I won't take part in delaying that file. If I'm asked, I'll say no.

I hope we can still work together. I'm still grateful. I'm just seeing you more clearly.

Parveen

qa.q: What did Eshaan sir call Advocate Sheikh?
qa.a: He called her "a nobody who got lucky".

qa.q: How did Parveen feel after overhearing Eshaan sir?
qa.a: Parveen felt let down and disillusioned after looking up to him more than anyone.

qa.q: How does Parveen set a boundary without discarding the mentor?
qa.a: Parveen thanks him sincerely, names what was wrong, and refuses to take part in delaying the file, while keeping what he taught.

qa.q: How might Eshaan sir feel reading this letter?
qa.a: He may feel embarrassed and defensive, but perhaps also respect Parveen's honesty.

grounding: A letter shows a young lawyer let down by a mentor's petty and unfair conduct, who keeps the true lessons, sees him as human and sets a clear boundary.
